newsitem.title: USA: ABC, producer hit with $10 million judgment.
newsitem.headline: ABC, producer hit with $10 million judgment.

text.p: A Miami jury on Wednesday awarded damages of $10 million to a Florida bank and its chief executive, who said he was libelled by ABC News in a television broadcast about real estate investments.

The judgment was the second major setback for ABC news programmes in 16 months. In August 1995, the network settled a $10 billion libel suit brought by two tobacco giants over a report accusing them of raising nicotine levels in cigarettes.
The U.S. District Court jury deliberated for four days before returning the judgment on Wednesday in favour of BankAtlantic Chairman Alan Levan and the company, Levan's attorney, Alan Fein, said.
The panel ruled that ABC, a subsidiary of Walt Disney Co., and its producer William Willson owed Levan $8.75 million and BankAtlantic $1.25 million.
"I think justice was done today," Fein said. "The jury saw a wrong and tried to right it."

As part of its 1995 settlement with Philip Morris and R.J. Reynolds, ABC issued an apology, saying it should not have reported on its newsmagazine "Day One" that the companies spiked cigarettes with nicotine. The network conceded it had made a mistake but said it was not deliberate.

After Wednesday's judgment, ABC said in a terse statement that it was "extremely disppointed" by the verdict and would contest it. "We believe the case was wrongly decided and intend to pursue our appeal rights vigorously," ABC said.

Levan sued Capital Cities/ABC News over a programme segment called "Too Good to Be True," aired on the network's "20/20" programme in November 1991. The story focused on a controversial swap of real estate partnerships for bonds at BankAtlantic Financial Corp.

The bank holding company acquired partnership interests in exchange for company bonds in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It then sold much of the underlying property, using some of the proceeds to help strengthen Fort Lauderdale-based BankAtlantic.

Levan had sought $20 million, alleging that the newsmagazine had ruined his reputation by mischaracterizing the deals, ensuring he would never again be able to deal in real estate limited partnerships.

U.S. District Judge C. Clyde Atkins ruled earlier in the trial, which last about six weeks, that Levan could not seek punitive damages against ABC News because there was no evidence ABC had displayed ill will against Levan.
Fein said he would contest that ruling in the future.
Levan said the lawsuit had been a matter of principle and vindication for what he called "irresponsible journalism."
"ABC News painted a picture about me and BankAtlantic which was not true and which caused us enormous damage," Levan said at a news conference after the judgment.
"What started as a serious journalistic effort really ran amok in the process ... and that's a terrible thing," he said.
Fein said BankAtlantic customers had closed accounts and called Levan a "crook" as a result of the broadcast.
Joseph Angotti, a journalism professor at the University of Miami, said libel judgments were difficult to obtain, because plaintiffs had to prove malicious intent.
He called the judgment against Willson, the ABC producer, rare and said it was bound to send shock waves through the television newsmagazine industry.

"It will have a very sobering effect on producers, who have always thought that if they do something wrong, their companies would have to pay the damages," Angotti said. "This is going to shake the industry."

ABC is also contesting a lawsuit in Greensboro, North Carolina. The network and four of its producers were sued for $1.7 billion in damages by Food Lion Inc., which claimed ABC committed civil fraud and other offences during an undercover investigation for a "PrimeTime Live" show.
